summary:
Botswana decriminalised consensual same-sex conduct through its own courts. The High Court struck down the colonial-era "carnal knowledge" offence on 11 June 2019 in Letsweletse Motshidiemang v Attorney General, and the Court of Appeal upheld that judgment on 29 November 2021.

Penal Code Section 167, which addresses same-sex conduct between women, was not removed by that litigation. In the Universal Periodic Review of May 2023 (43rd session), Botswana declined Canada's recommendation to repeal Section 167.

Legal gender recognition has been won case by case rather than granted by statute. In 2017 the High Court ordered the state to change a trans man's identity documents from female to male on dignity and humanity grounds (ND v Attorney General), and the same year Tshepo Ricki Kgositau obtained a female identity card after a four-year legal battle, the first court-ordered recognition of a trans woman's gender in Botswana. No general legal gender recognition statute exists, and at the 2023 Universal Periodic Review Botswana did not accept a recommendation to introduce an administrative process for it; the review records that a clear administrative process was yet to be introduced.

Community infrastructure is legally protected. The Court of Appeal ordered the state to register LEGABIBO in 2016 on freedom of association, expression and assembly grounds, and the organisation now runs advocacy, awareness, sexual-health and HIV programming together with coming-out, legal and support resources.

A draft constitutional amendment considered in 2024 would add discrimination protection for intersex persons and people with disabilities. In June 2024 deliberations the Minister of Labour and Home Affairs told legislators to keep "intersex" and "same-sex" distinct, and civic groups criticise the wider review process.

Implementation lags the judgments. Southern African Litigation Centre reported on 20 May 2024 that compliance with these precedent rulings "has not been satisfactory so far".

For a visitor: conduct decriminalised, courts functioning and willing to order the state, identity documents obtainable through litigation rather than administration, and continuing societal discrimination documented in official reporting.
tangentialFactors:
Botswana's judicial record on sexual-orientation and gender-identity cases is the strongest on the continent after South Africa, and the courts have repeatedly been the route by which rights were obtained rather than the legislature.

Human Rights Watch previewed the constitutional challenge to the "carnal knowledge" law on 24 January 2018 with the hearing set for March 2018, placing the 2019 and 2021 rulings in a multi-year litigation sequence that also confirmed the trans legal-gender right between 2017 and 2022.

The US State Department's 2011 Human Rights Report for Botswana documented same-sex conduct as then criminalised and recorded societal discrimination against LGBT people; that report predates the decriminalisation rulings and describes the earlier legal position.

Official caution persists alongside the case law. The Minister of Labour and Home Affairs' instruction to legislators in June 2024 to keep "intersex" and "same-sex" distinct indicates that protection is being extended in segments rather than as a single package, and civic groups criticise the constitutional review process itself.

At the same Universal Periodic Review session Botswana also declined a recommendation to decriminalise abortion, an adjacent marker of how the government handled rights recommendations in 2023.
localsOnly:
Residents have no administrative route to change gender markers on identity documents. Recognition is obtained by going to court, as in ND v Attorney General (2017) and Tshepo Ricki Kgositau's 2017 victory, and the 2023 Universal Periodic Review confirms that a clear administrative process was yet to be introduced.

Penal Code Section 167, covering same-sex conduct between women, remains unrepealed by statute; the 2019 decriminalisation ruling concerned the "carnal knowledge" provision, and the government declined to accept a recommendation to repeal Section 167 in 2023.

LEGABIBO is the principal national LGBTIQ+ organisation, registered under the 2016 Court of Appeal order, and provides advocacy, awareness campaigns, sexual-health and HIV work including World AIDS Day commemorations such as the 2017 event in Bobonong, alongside coming-out, law and constitution, and help and support resources.

The draft constitutional amendment would write discrimination protection for intersex persons and people with disabilities into the constitution, and its treatment in the 2024 legislative deliberations is being contested by civic groups.

Southern African Litigation Centre's assessment of May 2024 is that compliance with the landmark rulings has not been satisfactory, so a right confirmed in court may not be delivered consistently by the administration.
outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: whether Penal Code Section 167 has been used in prosecutions since the 2019 and 2021 rulings is not sourced in this inventory; the inventory establishes only that it was not repealed and that Botswana declined the repeal recommendation in 2023.

Unresolved: whether the draft 2024 constitutional amendment was enacted is not sourced here; the inventory covers the proposal and the June 2024 deliberations only.

Unresolved: Southern African Litigation Centre's finding that implementation "has not been satisfactory" is not broken down in this inventory by which specific orders went unimplemented, and it covers Namibia as well as Botswana.

Not sourced: there are no statistics or dated case records on physical violence against trans people in Botswana in this inventory. The 2011 US State Department report records societal discrimination but predates decriminalisation and should not be read as current.
